name: Berberism
summary: Berberism (Amazigh activism) is the North African movement for recognition of Berber identity, history and languages, chiefly in Morocco and Algeria. Its core demands are official status and schooling for Tamazight, an end to Arabisation, a rewritten national history and development of marginalised Berber regions. In Algeria the Kabyle strand also pressed for pluralist democracy and secularism against single-party and Islamist politics, while the Moroccan strand has mostly worked within the monarchy.
scope: The mainstream cultural, linguistic and democratic Amazigh rights movement since the late 1960s: Mouloud Mammeri's circle, the 1980 Berber Spring and the Kabyle MCB, RCD and FFS tradition in Algeria, and Morocco's Agadir Charter (1991) and Amazigh Manifesto (2000). It excludes the separatist MAK wing, Canarian Berber-symbol nationalism, and Tuareg politics. Economic and social-policy questions are mostly not addressed by the movement, so many answers are low-confidence inferences.

keyFigures.name: Mouloud Mammeri
keyFigures.role: Kabyle writer whose banned 1980 lecture triggered the Berber Spring and who founded the Berber academy in Paris.

keyFigures.name: Mohamed Chafik
keyFigures.role: Moroccan Amazigh intellectual credited with writing the 2000 Berber Manifesto.

sources.title: Charte d'Agadir relative aux droits linguistiques et culturels (1991)
sources.author: Moroccan Amazigh associations
sources.usedFor: Pluralist Moroccan identity, critique of the centralised unitary state, and demands for constitutional recognition, schooling, media and research.

sources.title: Manifeste berbère (2000)
sources.author: Amazigh signatories, Morocco
sources.usedFor: Nine demands: official status, teaching, history rewrite, regional development, media, names, and a brotherhood framing of Amazighs and Arabs.

sources.title: Berberism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Strands, MCB goals of Western-style democracy, secularism, opposition to Islamists and Arabisation, MAK separatism, state responses.

sources.title: Berber Spring
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: 1980 uprising as a challenge to FLN single-party rule and Arabisation, state repression, RCD and MCB legacy.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The Manifesto asks for priority state development of marginalised Berber regions, from which a mild preference for state-guaranteed basic services is inferred; healthcare is never addressed.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: The sources discuss regional neglect but no wage policy, and adherents span left and liberal parties, so no direction can be inferred.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The movement takes no economic doctrine; its demands for state development programmes in Berber regions point both ways.

public-ownership.rationale: Nothing in the charters concerns ownership of industry; adherents are split across left and liberal parties.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Taxation is never raised in the movement's texts, and its parties differ on economics.

unions-good.rationale: Unions and students joined the 1980 strikes, but labour organisation is not a Berberist theme; the answer is inferred only from that alliance.

property-fundamental.rationale: Property rights are not addressed; the nearest concern, land and regional resources, is a development demand rather than a property doctrine.

regulate-corporations.rationale: No position on corporate regulation appears in the charters or the scholarship used.

cut-welfare.rationale: Welfare policy is outside the movement's concerns; the call for state investment in neglected regions leans slightly against cuts but not enough to commit.

worker-ownership.rationale: Not a Berberist theme; no source links the movement to worker ownership.

surveillance-ok.rationale: The movement was itself policed and suppressed by security services under single-party rule, so adherents likely distrust surveillance powers; inferred.

legalize-drugs.rationale: The movement is silent on drug policy and strands (conservative rural, secular urban) would differ.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The Manifesto condemns Arabisation as ethnocide but asks for no speech restrictions; adherents are not documented as taking a side.

strong-leader.rationale: The 1980 Berber Spring was the first mass challenge to the FLN single-party system, and the movement demands pluralism over personal rule.

state-harmful.rationale: The Charter asks the state to constitutionally recognise and fund Amazigh language, so adherents want a better state, not none.

limit-guns.rationale: Gun control does not feature in the movement; no basis for a position.

empower-police-military.rationale: Police and army repressed the 1980 protests in Kabylia, so adherents are unlikely to want more state coercive power; inferred.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Not addressed; the movement is a cultural-rights cause with no stated sexual-morality line.

decide-locally.rationale: The Charter blames a centralised unitary state model for ignoring Amazigh rights, and Berberists favour regional recognition, though the texts stop short of demanding federalism.

rehabilitation.rationale: Penal philosophy never appears in the Charter, the Manifesto or the Berber Spring record, so there is no stated view on rehabilitation versus punishment.

traditional-family.rationale: Adherents range from secular urbanites to rural traditional communities, and no source gives a line.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Not addressed; Kabyle secularists might be sympathetic but the mainstream movement avoids the issue and the societies concerned are socially conservative, so a mild inferred no.

abortion-legal.rationale: Not addressed by the movement and adherents are split between secular and traditional currents.

more-religion-public.rationale: The MCB and Izegzawen sought political secularism and opposed Islamists, though the Manifesto avoids attacking Islam itself.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: The Manifesto demands rewriting history and redress for the neglect of Amazigh people, which is ethnic rather than racial redress; inferred from that.

gender-social-construct.rationale: No source gives a Berberist line on gender theory.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Preserving and promoting Amazigh culture is the core demand, though Berberists understand the national culture as plural rather than as a single tradition.

gradual-change.rationale: Activists petition within the system but also mounted strikes and protests; no doctrine on pace.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Berberism is about indigenous North African identity in Morocco and Algeria and has no immigration platform, so no direction can be inferred.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The Charter appeals to Morocco's international rights commitments, so adherents lean towards international norms; inferred.

free-trade.rationale: The Manifesto asks for regional development but says nothing about trade policy, so this is left neutral.

nation-first.rationale: The movement frames itself by minority rights and the Charter invokes international commitments, which leans away from nation-first; inferred.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Foreign military intervention is outside the concerns of a cultural-rights movement; nothing in the sources lets a stance be inferred.

open-borders.rationale: Not addressed; the transnational Amazigh idea concerns kin across the Maghreb, not migration policy generally.

limit-growth.rationale: Environmental limits are not discussed; the Manifesto wants economic development of Berber regions.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Climate policy is absent from the movement's documents, so no stance is recorded.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The movement takes no view on technological progress; its texts concern language, history and recognition.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Energy policy is never mentioned in Berberist texts, so this stays neutral.

revolution-justified.rationale: The movement mostly pursued reform and protest, while the MAK diaspora wing seeks independence; adherents are split.

experts-over-public.rationale: The Manifesto asks for an independent national commission of historians to set the curriculum, but this is not a general technocratic stance.

central-planning.rationale: Berberists opposed the FLN's centralised one-party state, which ran a planned economy, so mild opposition is inferred.

socialized-markets.rationale: The movement has no theory of ownership, and adherents sit in both socialist and liberal parties.

land-value-tax.rationale: Tax design is not discussed by Berberist sources, so no stance is inferable.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Inheritance taxation is absent from the Charter and the Manifesto.

basic-income.rationale: Welfare design is not a Berberist theme; no source gives a position.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Trade protection is not discussed; the Manifesto's development demand is regional, not tariff-based.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The Manifesto asks for a priority state development programme (infrastructure, agriculture, industry) for Berber regions, so adherents accept state direction of investment there.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Property structure is not part of the programme; the Manifesto's agricultural development demand does not specify ownership.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The movement's economic demands are for development within existing economies, so abolition is far outside it; inferred.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Monetary institutions never appear in Berberist sources.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Corporatist state bodies resemble the single-party system that Berberists challenged; inferred.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Berber Spring challenged FLN single-party rule, and Berberists sought pluralist democracy in its place.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Moroccan Berberists work within the monarchy and the Manifesto expresses trust in the King, while Algerian Berberists are republican, so the movement is split.

democracy-best.rationale: The MCB aimed at Western-style democracy and pluralism, and the Charter describes its aim as a democratic national culture.

direct-votes.rationale: No documented position on referendums; the movement stresses representation and pluralism.

workers-councils.rationale: Berberists want parliamentary pluralism; councils are not part of the programme.

right-to-secede.rationale: The MAK and some diaspora groups favour Kabyle independence, but most Berberist movements seek only cultural and linguistic rights. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

natural-rulers.rationale: The Manifesto's insistence on equal recognition of all Moroccans and its opposition to an Arabising hegemony imply rejection of natural hierarchy.

political-violence-never.rationale: Mainstream activists use protest and petition, but repression and the MAK's maximalism leave adherents divided.

war-builds-character.rationale: No source supports this; the movement is a civic and cultural cause, so mild rejection is inferred.

separate-church-state.rationale: The MCB and Izegzawen sought political secularism, though in Morocco the Manifesto avoids confronting Islam, so the answer is a clear but not maximal yes. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Berberist secularists oppose Islamist law-making and the Manifesto argues Arabic is not required for Muslim identity; some rural adherents are religiously observant. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The movement asks the state to provide recognition and services, so privatised justice is unlikely; inferred.

military-superiority.rationale: The movement has no foreign or defence policy, so this is left neutral.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The Charter and the Manifesto describe Moroccan identity as plural (Amazigh, Arab-Islamic, African) and call Amazigh and Arabs brothers within one nation.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Not a Berberist theme; the movement reads history through identity and language.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The movement demands equal recognition of language and culture, not equal material outcomes, so no stance on this is recorded.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Berberists claim to be the indigenous people of North Africa, and the Manifesto wants regional development and respect for place names, but the texts do not ask for authority over land.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Berberists reject the view that their identity is a colonial invention, but reparations are not a stated demand.

civilizational-union.rationale: Berberism rejects Arab-Muslim unification and pan-Arabism that would subsume Amazigh identity.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Moral philosophy of self-interest is not a Berberist theme.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The Charter frames its case as rights, citing international commitments, so duty-first communitarianism is unlikely; inferred.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Environmental ethics is absent from the movement's documents.

limit-population.rationale: Population policy is not discussed by the movement.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The Manifesto demands industrial and agricultural development of Berber regions; inferred rejection.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Berberist sources say nothing on accelerating technological disruption.

human-enhancement.rationale: Bioethics is outside the movement's concerns.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Automation of governance is not discussed in any source used.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Not addressed; the movement faced surveillance but never took a position on encryption.

restore-past-order.rationale: Berberism looks back to ancient Amazigh roots for identity but asks for modern institutions, democracy and standardised language, so it is not a restoration programme.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The sources describe a cause rather than a method of policy evaluation, so no stance is recorded.

direct-action.rationale: Berber Spring involved strikes and demonstrations, but activists and parties also contest elections (RCD, FFS).

means-match-ends.rationale: No source states a view on prefigurative methods; activists used strikes, petitions and party politics.

return-to-foraging.rationale: The Manifesto asks for modern development of Berber regions; the idea is far from the movement.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Outside the movement's concerns and at odds with its development demands; inferred.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Distributive principles are not addressed by the movement.

production-for-use.rationale: The movement has no stance on profit versus need as the basis of production.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Marxian exploitation theory is not a Berberist doctrine and the sources never use it.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Berberists contested one-party dictatorship and demand pluralism, so rule by one class is rejected. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

collective-farming.rationale: The Manifesto asks to develop Berber agriculture, which is mostly smallholder; collectivisation is not part of the movement; inferred.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Berberism's texts do not analyse capitalism or imperialism.

taxation-theft.rationale: The movement asks the state to fund and organise Amazigh education and media, which implies accepting taxation; inferred.

harm-principle.rationale: Berberist sources do not state a general liberty doctrine.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The movement claims group linguistic and cultural rights for Amazigh people, which cuts against the view that rights belong only to individuals.

conscription.rationale: Military service is not discussed in Berberist sources.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Berberists demand voice (democracy, pluralism) rather than exit, apart from MAK secessionists; inferred.

state-as-business.rationale: The Charter treats the state as a duty-bearer for rights, not a service firm; inferred.

positive-liberty.rationale: The movement does not take sides in this philosophical debate, though its development demands touch on material means.

media-academia-power.rationale: Not addressed, though the Manifesto does want media and universities to change.

hereditarian-race.rationale: The Manifesto describes Amazighs and Arabs as brothers in one identity and rejects hegemonic ideology; racial hierarchy runs against it.

organic-representation.rationale: Berberists want party pluralism and democracy; corporative representation is not part of their programme.

total-state.rationale: The movement was formed in resistance to a state that imposed Arabisation in all areas of life.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Not a stated aim; Berberism is about recognition within existing states, so rejection is inferred.

national-rebirth.rationale: Berberism seeks a cultural revival but not a nationalist rebirth against decadence.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Berberists oppose personalist rule and demand pluralist democracy.

bound-labor.rationale: Contrary to any development programme and to a democratic rights platform.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The Manifesto argues that official history is a product of the Arabising state and must be rewritten, which implies knowledge reflects power; inferred.

universal-morality.rationale: The Charter appeals to international human-rights commitments, implying universal norms; inferred.

single-common-good.rationale: Berberism is pluralist about identities and interests, which cuts against a single common good.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: The movement has no unified view; some Amazigh activists have sought contact with Israel, while others are pro-Palestinian.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Return rights are not addressed; Berberism treats North Africa as home, not a diaspora homeland.

revive-national-language.rationale: The Manifesto and the Charter demand standardising, teaching and official status for Tamazight, but Tamazight is still spoken daily by millions, so the statement about reviving a language that has fallen out of use fits only partly.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Corporate governance is not a Berberist theme.

school-vouchers.rationale: The Charter wants Amazigh in public schools, which implies public provision, but vouchers are not discussed.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Macroeconomic policy is not discussed by the movement.

economic-freedom.rationale: Berberists link political pluralism with freedom, but no source ties it to economic freedom.

rule-by-example.rationale: Berberists seek constitutional and legal guarantees for rights rather than moral exemplars.

national-self-determination.rationale: Berberists claim a right to cultural and linguistic self-assertion, while only some, such as the MAK, take this to statehood.

force-without-un.rationale: Foreign-policy use of force is outside the movement's documents.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Kabyle secularists lean rationalist, but the Moroccan strand avoids religious debate; split.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Welfare eligibility is not addressed; the movement's sources do not take up immigration.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Workfare conditions are not a Berberist topic.

class-collaboration.rationale: Class relations are not analysed; the movement organises on identity and language.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Preserving and reviving a threatened heritage is the movement's purpose. The sources set out the underlying principle but do not state a position on this specific statement.

dominated-front.rationale: Berberism rejects Arab-nationalist and Islamist fronts, though anti-Western sentiment is not its theme; inferred.

workers-nation.rationale: Not part of the movement; a national class stance conflicts with its minority-rights framing; inferred.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Kabyle secular currents want equal rights, though rural conservative strands exist; not a documented position.

ban-interest.rationale: Islamist economics is associated with the Islamist camp that Berberists oppose; inferred.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Berberism demands equal recognition and describes Amazigh and Arabs as brothers. The sources set out the underlying principle but do not state a position on this specific statement.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Not a Berberist analysis; they see the state as an instrument of Arabisation, not of a class.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Energy production policy never appears in the sources.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Berberists reject forced assimilation as ethnocide, though the statement concerns immigrants and is not addressed directly. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

elite-replacement.rationale: The Manifesto rejects hegemonic ideologies and conspiracy talk is not part of the movement.

proportional-representation.rationale: Berberists sought pluralist parliaments and minority representation; PR is inferred rather than demanded.

national-mission.rationale: Spreading a national form of government plays no role in Berberism, which is concerned with recognition inside existing states; a mild no is inferred.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Not addressed; the movement is split between secular feminists and traditional strands.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Contrary to the equal-dignity framing of the Manifesto.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: The state killed about 128 people in 1980 and the movement demands justice for Kabylia, though this is not formalised in the sources; inferred.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The movement asks the state to enact language rights, schooling and media, which is far from a minimal state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: The Manifesto declares Amazighs and Arabs brothers within a single identity. The sources set out the underlying principle but do not state a position on this specific statement.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Manifesto declares equal recognition and the Charter invokes international rights.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Debates in Marxist theory are not part of Berberism.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Berberists do see Arab conquest as a source of identity loss but consensus is lacking and sources do not state this.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Secular Berberists favour a common civil law, though the Moroccan strand avoids it; inferred.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Secularist currents oppose such limits; Moroccan strand silent; inferred.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: This Hindu-nationalist demand has no connection to the movement.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The Manifesto argues Arabic is not required for Muslim identity but does not demand removing religious teaching.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The movement demands democratic pluralism and recognition by the state, which implies legitimacy through consent.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist trade aims are not discussed by Berberist sources.

population-transfer.rationale: The Manifesto condemns Arabisation as ethnocide against Amazighs and calls for brotherhood among Moroccans. The sources set out the underlying principle but do not state a position on this specific statement.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Libertarian non-aggression is not a Berberist doctrine; adherents are split on the use of force.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Not a Berberist theme; their politics concerns plural coexistence; inferred.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Berberists oppose Islamist parties, but they were themselves banned (Amazigh Democratic Party, 2007) under a similar logic, so are split.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The Manifesto speaks of hegemonic domination of Amazigh by Arabising policy, which fits this idea; inferred.

separated-powers.rationale: The movement wants democracy and independent commissions (the Manifesto asks for an independent history commission); inferred.

vanguard-party.rationale: Berberists challenged single-party rule and favour pluralism.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The Manifesto prioritises marginalised, mostly rural Berber regions, which suggests this orientation.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: British-style housing policy has no counterpart in Berberist sources.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Strikes were central to the Berber Spring, so adherents are unlikely to support restrictions; inferred.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: The causes of poverty are not analysed in the movement's texts beyond regional neglect.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The Charter holds that recognising multiple dimensions builds national culture, and that suppressing them harms the whole people.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Sortition is never mentioned in Berberist sources.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The 1980 repression and later emergency rules in Algeria affected Kabylia; inferred rejection.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Price regulation is not part of the movement's agenda.

party-controls-media.rationale: The Manifesto asks for dedicated Berber broadcasting and press support, which means opposing state monopoly over information. The sources set out the underlying principle but do not state a position on this specific statement.

party-commands-army.rationale: Berberists oppose single-party control of the state.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Naturalisation rules are not discussed in the sources.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Politician pay is not a Berberist issue.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Party organisation is not covered by the sources; Kabyle parties (FFS, RCD) are rivals, not a single disciplined body.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Not addressed; Amazigh solidarity across states is cultural, and the Charter notes Amazigh speakers from Egypt to the Canaries.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Moroccan strand accepts a monarchy that commands the forces, Algerian strand is republican; unclear.

church-by-bishops.rationale: The statement concerns Christian church governance, which has no equivalent in this movement.

clerical-rule.rationale: The MCB and Izegzawen sought political secularism against the Islamist political sphere; this is documented for the Kabyle strand.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Revolutionary defeatism has no place in the sources.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The Manifesto calls for reviving Berber arts beyond folklore and equal support, so moral censorship is opposed.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Berberists contest unchecked, entrenched power such as the FLN's.

recall-officials.rationale: The sources do not discuss recall mechanisms, though they favour democracy generally.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Defence alliances are outside the movement's concerns.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Not addressed; inferred rejection as extreme.

people-in-arms.rationale: Armed citizenry is not discussed by Berberist sources.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The Manifesto defends rural Berber regions and heritage, but it also demands their development, so it is not an anti-urban doctrine.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Some activists look to transnational Amazigh unity, as the Charter notes speakers across the Maghreb, but mainstream Berberism operates within existing states. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Berberism was led by intellectuals, students and academics such as Mammeri; inferred rejection.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: The Charter argues Amazigh culture is one of several constituent dimensions that deserves equal standing; the claim that Amazigh is the oldest culture suggests some pride, but equality of recognition is the demand.

death-penalty.rationale: Capital punishment is not a Berberist theme, and adherents' views are not documented.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: School curriculum demands concern language and history, not sex education.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Secular Berberists oppose religion in schools; inferred.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Sexual-content regulation is not covered by Berberist sources.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Berberism sees citizenship as common to all in the state, not by blood; inferred.

minority-language-support.rationale: The Manifesto and the Charter explicitly demand schooling, media, courts, administration and elections support for Tamazight.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Exemptions from general law for religious minorities are not discussed in the sources.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Millian individuality is not a Berberist position.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: International debt is not discussed by the movement.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Berberism seeks recognition rather than decolonisation of property systems, so this theory is not part of it.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The Charter and Manifesto ask for constitutional recognition of Tamazight; a democratically elected constituent process is not stated but follows from calls for national debate.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Berberists demand political freedom against single-party rule. The sources set out the underlying principle but do not state a position on this specific statement.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Global aid duties are outside the movement's documents.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Nuclear strategy is not discussed in any source used.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The sources do not say how heads of state should be chosen.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Land-for-peace is not a Berberist issue; activists differ on the Middle East.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The movement states no theory of property.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: This debate within Marxism is not part of Berberism.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental regulation is not a topic in Berberist documents.

collective-defense.rationale: Alliance obligations are not addressed by the movement.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: The movement has no position on annexation in general.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Berberist secularists want religion out of politics, but the aim is not clerical subordination.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Berberist sources do not discuss the role of a head of state.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Berberists object to state coercion against Kabylia; MAK secessionists would oppose force outright; inferred.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Regional autonomy for Kabylia and Amazigh regions is a common demand, although not in the cited charters; inferred.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Secular-leaning Berberists reject sacral kingship, but the Moroccan strand works within the sharifian monarchy.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Income tax structure is not a Berberist theme.

character-from-environment.rationale: The nature-nurture question is not addressed.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Berberists contest unaccountable ruling power; inferred from the demand for pluralism.

space-expansion.rationale: Space policy is irrelevant to the movement.

mixed-constitution.rationale: The sources do not discuss classical constitutional theory.

leader-cult.rationale: Berberists opposed the FLN's one-party personalism and demanded democracy.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Maoist doctrine with no counterpart in Berberism.

land-redistribution.rationale: The Manifesto demands development of Berber regions but does not ask for expropriating estates.

refugee-return.rationale: Refugee return is not a Berberist topic.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Berberism seeks recognition within existing states, not territorial claims; inferred.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Secularist Berberists oppose religious penal law, as the MCB and Izegzawen sought political secularism.

women-must-cover.rationale: Secularists oppose religious dress laws and the Manifesto argues for pluralism.

common-currency.rationale: Currency union is not discussed by the sources.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: The Charter notes Amazigh speakers across the Maghreb, but the movement does not demand cross-border political unity; some activists are for it. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: The Manifesto and Charter ask for Amazigh schools, media and institutes within the state rather than separate statehood; the MAK dissents.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Berberists claim equal rights in Algeria and Morocco as their indigenous lands and reject migration out.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Berberism reads history through identity and language, not historical materialism, and takes no formal position here.

ban-cartels.rationale: Competition law is not covered by the movement's sources.

no-bailouts.rationale: Financial rescue policy is outside the movement.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Berberists are a minority demanding that majorities not override recognised rights; they appeal to international commitments.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Not addressed; secular strands would be sympathetic, conservatives not.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Autarkic blocs are far from the Manifesto's call for development of Berber regions, though it never rules out protection; mild rejection inferred.

moral-incentives.rationale: Work incentives are not a Berberist subject.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Mainstream Berberism pursued civic mobilisation and pluralism; foco theory was not part of it.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Not addressed; split between republican Algeria and monarchical Morocco.

history-own-civilization.rationale: The Manifesto demands rewriting the history curriculum to centre the Amazigh role in Moroccan history.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Berberism rejects Arabisation as ethnocide imposed by a hegemonic ideology. The sources set out the underlying principle but do not state a position on this specific statement.

patriotic-education.rationale: The Manifesto wants national history revised, but not flag loyalty.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Affirmative action is a US debate with no analogue in the sources; the Manifesto asks for equal support, not quotas.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Crisis theory is not part of Berberism.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Berberists reject Arab and Ottoman imperial narratives and consider French influence an issue; inferred rejection.

delink-world-market.rationale: The Manifesto asks for economic development of Berber regions, which implies integration rather than delinking.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Leninist imperialism theory is absent from Berberist sources.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The Manifesto demands equal treatment for Amazigh people and artists.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The Charter demands constitutional recognition and cites international rights commitments, which implies entrenched protection for minority rights.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: The Berberist view on colonial borders is not documented.

elective-rulers.rationale: Berberists back democracy but the Moroccan strand operates within a monarchy. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

minority-veto.rationale: Berberism seeks recognition through constitutional and democratic channels, and the sources do not mention minority vetoes.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The Berber Spring challenged an unaccountable regime; inferred.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Berberists seek parliamentary democracy and pluralism; inferred.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Animal ethics is not discussed in the sources.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Animal welfare policy is not discussed in the sources.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Aristocratic obligations are not part of the movement's thought.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The movement is activist and political by definition. The sources set out the underlying principle but do not state a position on this specific statement.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Critical theory of mass culture is not a Berberist position.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Gramscian analysis is not used in Berberist sources; they instead describe state imposition of Arabisation.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Dependency theory is not part of the movement, which stresses internal regional neglect.

native-born-offices.rationale: Berberism asks for equal recognition for all Moroccans and Algerians and a plural nation; inferred.

party-own-road.rationale: Communist-party autonomy is not a Berberist concern.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Development strategy beyond regional investment is not specified.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Irredentism is not a stated aim; Berberism works within existing borders.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Berberists claim indigeneity but the movement does not seek rule over Arabs, whom the Manifesto calls brothers.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Constitutional values of this kind are not discussed by the movement, whose own constitutional demand concerns language.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Historical equivalence debates are not part of Berberism.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: An American historical dispute with no connection to the movement.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Monument politics are not discussed, though the Manifesto does ask for institutions to be named after Moroccan historical figures.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Gender-equity policy is not a Berberist topic.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Domestic-violence services are not addressed by the sources.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: The MCB wanted Western-style democracy, which suggests rejecting civilisational exceptionalism for institutions.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The army was a pillar of the regime that repressed Kabylia; inferred.

paid-care-work.rationale: Care labour is not discussed in the sources.

filial-duty.rationale: Family ethics are not set out in Berberist documents; adherents range from traditional rural to secular urban.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Foreign investment policy is not part of the movement.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Family law reform is not addressed, and adherents are split between secular and traditional currents.

recallable-delegates.rationale: The sources do not discuss imperative mandates.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Pension design is outside the movement's concerns.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Community land tenure is not discussed, though Berber regions have customary tenures; no source states a position.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Parliamentary democracy is the movement's aim; inferred.

single-official-language.rationale: The Manifesto demands Tamazight as official alongside Arabic and opposes Arabisation.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Foreign land ownership is not discussed by the movement.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: US anti-discrimination doctrine has no analogue in the sources.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Consumer culture is not discussed by the movement.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Covert foreign policy is outside the movement's concerns; the Berberist cause is non-militarist, so a mild no is inferred.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Not addressed; implied by opposition to domination.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The Berber Spring protested against the FLN's one-party establishment, and Kabyle opposition parties campaign on democratisation, so distrust of ruling elites is likely; the sources do not state corruption claims.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist doctrine of the strengthened socialist state is alien to a movement that opposed one-party rule; inferred.

corporate-influence.rationale: Not addressed in the movement's texts; adherents span left and liberal parties.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Inferred: Amazigh associations depend on outside support and oppose states that suppress them.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Not addressed in the movement's texts.

residents-only-property.rationale: Not addressed; the Manifesto's concern is regional development, not property restriction.

job-guarantee.rationale: Not addressed; the movement takes no stance on employment policy.

democratic-peace.rationale: The MCB tradition sought Western-style democracy; the peace claim itself is inferred.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Not addressed; the movement works through law in Morocco and defied it in Algeria's Berber Spring, so it is split.

non-intervention.rationale: Not addressed in the movement's texts.

industrial-unions.rationale: Unions joined the 1980 strikes, but union form is not a Berberist theme.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The Manifesto frames Amazighs and Arabs as brothers; inferred rejection of conspiracy claims against minorities, which Berbers have themselves faced.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Not addressed; the secularist strand does not discuss marriage law.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Inferred from the pluralist democratic demands of the Kabyle strand.

local-production.rationale: Not addressed; development of Berber regions is a demand, but local production is not.

informal-organisation.rationale: Inferred: the MCB, RCD and FFS built formal parties and associations to press their demands.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Inferred: the movement appeals to international linguistic and cultural rights against national centralism.

religious-nation.rationale: The MCB wants secularism and opposes Islamist politics and Arabisation, so a religion-defined nation is rejected.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Inferred from the movement's demand for pluralism and equality of Amazighs and Arabs, which sits poorly with ritual primacy of a leading power.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: The Manifesto demands development of marginalised Berber regions and the Charter criticises the centralised state, from which regional control of resources is inferred.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Economic ownership questions are not addressed by the movement; adherents range from the socialist FFS tradition to liberals.

defeat-communism.rationale: The movement opposes single-party rule and Islamists, but it does not take a stand on communism as a world system.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle movement's pursuit of Western-style democracy, which accepts mixed provision; not addressed directly.

religion-illusion.rationale: The MCB pressed for secularism against Islamist politics, but Berbers are mostly Muslim and the movement does not make a materialist claim about religion.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Not addressed; the movement is cultural and democratic, and adherents are split on economics.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Inferred from the secular democratic strand, which pursues equality through law and rights rather than economic transformation.

socialized-care.rationale: Not addressed by the movement; no position on domestic and care work is documented.

purge-loanwords.rationale: The movement was itself a response to forced Arabisation and defends linguistic plurality, so purging loanwords is opposed by inference.

treaties-binding.rationale: Inferred from the movement's demand for constitutional recognition and legal guarantees of cultural rights, which implies lasting commitments.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle movement's aim of Western-style democracy and state institutions rather than communal reorganisation.

majority-settlement.rationale: The movement resists state assimilation and Arabisation and demands that Berber regions be governed and developed on their own terms.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Economic systems are not addressed by the movement, so no third-way position is documented.

historical-land-claim.rationale: The Manifesto grounds Amazigh claims in the people's being indigenous to North Africa long before Arabisation.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Inferred from the movement's democratic and humanist character; not discussed in the sources.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The Kabyle strand is secular and pluralist, but the sources do not discuss homosexuality, so inferred.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The Kabyle MCB, RCD and FFS pressed for pluralist democracy against single-party rule.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The Kabyle strand favoured secularism, and the Moroccan strand worked within the monarchy; this is inferred.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Inferred from the movement's complaints of internal colonisation and Arabisation; overseas territories are not discussed.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle opposition to Islamist politics; not discussed.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: The Kabyle strand opposed Islamist politics and sought pluralist democracy; inferred.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Inferred from the movement's grass-roots, cultural-association character; not stated.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: The sources do not discuss this, and adherents span left and liberal parties.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: The sources do not address gender identity and adherents span positions.

assisted-dying.rationale: Not addressed in the sources and no adherent position is known.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Not addressed; the movement is mostly about identity, not left-right.

alienated-labor.rationale: Economic theory is not addressed and adherents span left and liberal parties.

islam-incompatible.rationale: The movement seeks its own place within North Africa and Algeria's Kabyle strand is secular; inferred, with Islam itself not discussed.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle secularism against Islamist politics.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Kabyle secularists would likely back it, Moroccan strand split; inferred.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Inferred from the movement's rights-based, democratic demands; not discussed.

social-market-economy.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; adherents span left and liberal parties.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle demand for democratic, non-militarised politics; not discussed.

rich-first.rationale: The Manifesto asks for development of marginalised regions, which cuts against letting some regions grow rich first; inferred.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The Moroccan strand works within the monarchy and the Kabyle strand favours democracy; the sources do not address succession.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: The movement does not address banking or credit.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: The movement does not address foreign debt and its adherents span left and liberal parties.

property-franchise.rationale: The Manifesto and Kabyle strand demand pluralist democracy; a property franchise is inferred to be rejected, though not mentioned.

domination-women-nature.rationale: The sources never address gender or ecology.

reification.rationale: The movement does not address economic theory.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: The movement demands cultural and linguistic rights but does not discuss media ownership.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The Manifesto demands constitutional recognition and legal guarantees, from which a preference for fixed law is inferred.

racial-franchise.rationale: The movement opposes an Arab-ethnic definition of the nation and demands equal rights for all, Berbers included.

online-participation.rationale: The sources do not address the internet.

open-government-data.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle democratic strand's calls for transparency against the single-party state; not stated.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: The Kabyle strand pressed for secularism and pluralism, so legal limits on interfaith marriage are inferred to be rejected.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: The Kabyle strand's secular pluralism points against shunning a religious minority; inferred, not stated.

citizens-assembly.rationale: The movement's democratic strand favours pluralist politics, but nothing in the sources addresses sortition, so no position is inferred.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle strand's secularism and opposition to Islamist politics; the sources do not address religious reinterpretation directly.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The movement does not address wealth inequality; its social demands concern regional development, so no clear stance is inferred.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle MCB's goals of Western-style democracy and secularism; military service is never discussed.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The movement is secularist and pluralist rather than anti-religious, and the Manifesto frames Amazighs and Arabs as brothers; inferred.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Never addressed; the movement works through legal and constitutional reform and demands more state development, not abolition of state institutions.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The Agadir Charter criticises the centralised unitary state and demands recognition of Moroccan plurality, from which guaranteed shares for communities is inferred.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The Manifesto asks for a priority state programme for neglected regions, implying more reliance on state provision than on charity; inferred.

term-limits.rationale: Not addressed by the movement; no position can be inferred from its core demands.

vote-delegation.rationale: Not addressed; the movement seeks pluralist representative democracy and says nothing on delegable voting.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Never addressed; the movement's concerns are identity, language and regional development.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Inferred from the secular, democratic Kabyle strand's opposition to Islamist politics; religious office is not discussed.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Inferred from the movement's secular, Western-style democratic orientation; the Manifesto does not discuss marriage.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: The movement addresses language and culture; the sources do not discuss voting by foreign residents.

rent-control.rationale: Economic and social-policy questions are mostly not addressed by the movement; no source covers rents.

abolish-ip.rationale: Not addressed by the Agadir Charter or the Manifesto; left neutral.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle strand's pluralist, democratic and secular politics, opposed to single-party mobilisation of youth.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Not addressed by the movement; no source covers nuclear weapons.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Not addressed by the movement; no source covers foreign bases.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Inferred from the demand to rewrite national history to include Amazigh past and suffering; the sources do not discuss genocide recognition.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Economic questions of this kind are mostly not addressed by the movement.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The movement is largely non-violent but the sources do not take a position on lethal self-defence.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: The movement stresses Amazigh peoplehood as indigenous to North Africa since antiquity and demands a rewritten history reflecting that.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Victims of the 1980 Berber Spring are remembered, but sacred veneration of the nation's dead is not part of the movement; inferred.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The Kabyle strand pressed for secularism against Islamist politics, so a spiritual-struggle view of politics is not theirs.

culture-before-state.rationale: The movement's demands are chiefly cultural and linguistic recognition within existing states, rather than building a new state.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: The movement opposes Arabisation and the dominance of one ethnic identity, and demands equal recognition, which implies open economic roles; inferred.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: The Agadir Charter and Manifesto seek recognition and regional development, not a merged ethnic territory, and the separatist wing is excluded.

independent-unions.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle strand's pluralist democratic politics, which favours civil society independent of single-party control.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Not addressed by the movement, which concentrates on language and identity.

local-essentials-public.rationale: The Manifesto asks for priority state development of marginalised regions, from which support for public basic services is inferred.

municipal-property.rationale: Not addressed; the movement works within market and state economies and asks the state for development, not communal ownership.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Not addressed; some Kabyle voices favour federalism but this is not a defining demand.

online-anonymity.rationale: Inferred from activists' long experience of state repression and the importance of online spaces for Amazigh expression.

person-over-state.rationale: The Kabyle strand pressed for pluralist democracy and rights against single-party rule, implying individual rights over state ends.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Not addressed; the Kabyle strand is secular while Moroccan Amazigh activism is not hostile to religion.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: The Manifesto and Agadir Charter seek constitutional entrenchment of Tamazight and regional development, which implies protected rather than revocable powers.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The movement is organised on language, culture and history rather than race, and the Kabyle strand favours plural civic democracy.

racial-pride.rationale: Pride in Amazigh ancestry, history and language is central to the movement and its answer to Arabisation.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle democratic strand's rejection of militarised single-party states; wars of aggression are not part of its programme.

language-defines-nation.rationale: The Manifesto and Agadir Charter define the Amazigh as one people united by Tamazight language and history across the Moroccan and Algerian border, though the claim is about a people rather than a state.

communal-electorates.rationale: The movement seeks equal rights for citizens and secular pluralism in Algeria; separate religious electorates are inferred to be disfavoured.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: The mainstream movement is not framed around partition plots, though some Berberists accuse states of divide-and-rule; adherents are split.

free-public-college.rationale: The Manifesto seeks priority state education programmes for marginalised regions; free tuition is a low-confidence inference.

pollution-taxes.rationale: The movement does not address environmental taxation and adherents have no common line.

future-generations.rationale: Inferred from the movement's defence of heritage and its call for sustainable development of regions; not stated in the sources.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Berberist sources stress the equality of men and women, but do not claim distinct values for women; no clear line.

arms-reduction.rationale: Arms levels are not addressed by the movement and adherents would be split.

open-diplomacy.rationale: The Kabyle democratic strand pressed for pluralist democracy and transparency against single-party rule; open diplomacy is inferred.

capital-controls.rationale: The movement never addressed capital controls, and the Moroccan and Algerian strands differ in economics.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle democratic wing's opposition to armed Islamist groups; the movement does not address the arms question itself.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Inferred: the movement is cultural and democratic, and has no tradition of urging soldiers to defy orders; not addressed.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Inferred from the Manifesto's democratic and social-rights framing; labor bargaining is not addressed.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Economic policy of this kind is not addressed by the movement.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Fiscal policy is not addressed by the movement's charters.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Not addressed; the movement concerns identity and internal marginalisation rather than the international economic order.

smash-state-machine.rationale: The movement seeks recognition and reform within existing states through constitutional change, not replacement of the state machinery.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Not addressed; the movement has no economic blueprint.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Environmental accounting is not addressed by the movement.

sacred-nation.rationale: Inferred from the movement's emphasis on Amazigh history and identity as a lasting community; it does not use sacred language.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Student debt is not addressed by the movement.

internal-colonialism.rationale: The Manifesto and Charter describe Berber regions as marginalised by the Arab-centred state and call for their priority development, a close fit to the claim.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Inferred from the charters' appeal to universal human and cultural rights; not stated as a view of human nature.

public-service-media.rationale: The charters demand Tamazight in public media and education, implying support for public media; independence from government is not discussed.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Not addressed; the Kabyle strand is secularist while Moroccan Amazigh activism works within an Islamic monarchy.

farm-price-support.rationale: The Manifesto asks for priority development of agriculture in marginalised Berber regions, from which mild support for farm assistance is inferred.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Nuclear policy is never addressed by the movement.

workers-own-party.rationale: The movement is cultural and democratic, not class-based; no stance on separate workers' parties is documented.

ban-fgm.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle strand's pluralist, secular and human-rights democratic stance; the practice is not discussed.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Inferred from the movement's secular democratic and equal-rights stance; inheritance law is not specifically addressed.

one-language-many-names.rationale: The movement's central demand is that Tamazight, with its Kabyle, Tashelhit and Tarifit varieties, be recognised as one national language.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Inferred from the movement's preference for state-led development and democratic institutions; not addressed directly.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Inferred from the movement's secular democratic politics, which prefers elected over customary authority; not addressed directly.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: The movement does not address environmental priority versus liberty.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Inferred from the democratic, rights-based stance of the Kabyle strand; sentencing is not addressed.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Inferred by analogy from the movement's rejection of imposed Arabisation and its demand for linguistic pluralism.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: The movement is about language and identity, and its adherents span left and liberal parties, so no direction on union membership can be inferred.

voter-id.rationale: Not addressed by the Charter or Manifesto; electoral-administration rules are not a movement issue and adherents have no shared line.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Inferred from the movement's demand for equal recognition of Berber language and culture and, in the Kabyle strand, secularism against Islamist politics.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle strand's push for pluralist democracy against single-party rule; the sources do not define democracy procedurally.

premarital-sex.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the secular, liberal outlook of the Kabyle democratic strand, while Moroccan adherents are more mixed.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: Inferred from a rights movement that depends on open communication and has itself faced state repression; shutdowns are never discussed.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Social-policy questions are mostly not addressed by the movement, and adherents span left and liberal parties.

women-suffrage.rationale: Not discussed directly; inferred from the Manifesto's call for democracy and equal citizenship, which no adherent would exclude women from.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Not addressed; Kabyle secularists and Moroccan monarchy-friendly adherents would likely differ, so no direction is inferred.

race-social-construct.rationale: Inferred from the movement's framing of Berber identity as a matter of language, culture and history rather than biological race.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the democratic and secular strand's general support for state promotion of equality.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Not addressed by the movement, which concentrates on language and identity; no basis for a lean.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: Inferred from the Manifesto's human-rights and democratic framing; international criminal courts are not mentioned.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle strand's secularism; scripture is not discussed.

gendered-self-government.rationale: Inferred from the Manifesto's democratic and equal-rights language; not discussed for self-government.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle movement's opposition to single-party rule and Arab-socialist state ideology.

indirect-election.rationale: Inferred from the Kabyle pluralist-democracy demands; indirect election is not discussed.

national-church-status.rationale: Kabyle secularists and the Manifesto oppose a state religion, and Berberism rejects Arabo-Islamic uniformity in law.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: The Amazigh Manifesto and Kabyle parties press for regional autonomy or decentralisation for Berber regions.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Not addressed; the mainstream excludes the separatist wing and no source mentions plebiscites.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Inferred from the mainstream movement's work within existing states, setting aside the separatist wing; not discussed.

simple-living.rationale: Not addressed; the movement concerns identity and language, not lifestyle.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Inferred from the Berber claim to be North Africa's original inhabitants whose regions need protection; settlement is not discussed.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Amazigh activism stresses indigeneity and attachment to the Tamazgha homeland; the sources never state a spiritual duty to the land, so this is inferred.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: The pluralist, democratic Kabyle strand demands due process and rights; killing suspects without trial is never discussed, so this is inferred.

close-ties-china.rationale: The movement takes no position on great-power alignment; adherents span parties with different foreign orientations.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Berberism seeks rights within existing Moroccan and Algerian states rather than state sponsorship of kin across borders; inferred from its citizenship-based demands.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Natural-resource ownership is not addressed, and adherents span left and liberal parties.

self-ownership.rationale: Its pluralist, rights-based demands imply support for individual liberty, but self-ownership as a doctrine is not discussed, so this is inferred.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: No tax policy appears in the Charter or Manifesto, so no direction can be inferred.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: The Manifesto asks for state development of marginalised regions, which is neither clearly targeted nor universal.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: The Kabyle strand works through pluralist parties and associations and demands organised pluralism; direct leader rule is not part of its aims, so this is inferred.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Its critique of a centralised, unequal state suggests opposition to favouritism, but business privilege is never addressed.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: The Kabyle strand is secularist and the Moroccan strand stresses a shared identity across Arab and Amazigh lines; inferred, as Islamist-aligned adherents exist.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: The Manifesto couples cultural revival with regional development and modern schooling and media; inferred, as the question is not discussed.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: The secular, democratic strand supports gender equality, but divorce rights are not discussed in the sources, so this is inferred.

national-resource-control.rationale: The Manifesto's regional-development demand implies local benefit from resources, but resource control is not discussed; inferred.

missingStatements.text: Minority-language names for people and places should be legally recognised and protected.
missingStatements.rationale: The Manifesto demands an end to distorting or Arabising Berber place names and lifting the ban on Amazigh first names.

notes: The Moroccan strand works inside the monarchy and avoids confronting Islam; the Kabyle strand is republican and explicitly secular-democratic; the MAK wing seeks independence. Economic positions are not stated, so most economic answers are neutral or low-confidence.
